content: The report consolidates and summarizes all recommendations from the CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) regarding the prevention and control of tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis in the United States. It serves as a comprehensive resource for clinicians and public health providers, replacing all previously published reports and policy notes. No new recommendations are included in this document. ACIP recommends routine vaccination against tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis. Infants and young children should receive a 5-dose series of the diphtheria and tetanus toxoids and acellular pertussis (DTaP) vaccine, followed by a single adolescent booster dose of the tetanus toxoid, reduced diphtheria toxoid, and acellular pertussis (Tdap) vaccine. Adults who have never received Tdap are also advised to receive a booster dose of Tdap. Pregnant women are recommended to receive a dose of Tdap during each pregnancy, ideally between 27 and 36 weeks of gestation, regardless of prior Tdap vaccination history. After receiving Tdap, adolescents and adults should receive a booster dose of the tetanus and diphtheria toxoids (Td) vaccine every 10 years to maintain protection against tetanus and diphtheria. The ACIP develops recommendations for the routine use of vaccines in children, adolescents, and adults. These recommendations are harmonized with those of other professional organizations, such as the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), the American Academy of Family Physicians (AAFP), and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG). Once approved by the CDC Director, ACIP recommendations become official agency guidelines upon publication in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR). The report provides a historical overview of vaccination practices, including the transition from whole-cell pertussis vaccines (DTP) to acellular pertussis vaccines (DTaP) in the 1990s due to safety concerns. Since 1997, infants and young children have been recommended to receive a 5-dose series of DTaP. In 2005, ACIP recommended a single dose of Tdap for adolescents and adults. In 2012, to reduce the burden of pertussis in infants, ACIP recommended Tdap vaccination during each pregnancy. Pertussis, caused by Bordetella pertussis, is an acute respiratory disease characterized by three phases: catarrhal, paroxysmal, and convalescent. The catarrhal phase involves mild symptoms such as coryza, occasional cough, and low-grade fever. The paroxysmal phase is marked by spasmodic coughing, post-tussive vomiting, and inspiratory whooping. Symptoms gradually improve during the convalescent phase, which can last for weeks to months. Factors influencing the clinical presentation include age, immunity level, vaccination history, and early antimicrobial use. Tetanus is a life-threatening but vaccine-preventable disease caused by the neurotoxin Clostridium tetani. The bacterium is found in soil and animal excrement, and infection occurs through breaches in the skin or mucous membranes. The disease is characterized by muscle spasms and rigidity due to the production of tetanospasmin, a potent exotoxin. The incubation period varies from 3 to 21 days, with shorter periods associated with more severe disease. Tetanus is preventable through vaccination with tetanus toxoid-containing vaccines, such as DTaP, DT, Td, or Tdap. Diphtheria is an acute, communicable infectious illness caused by toxigenic strains of Corynebacterium diphtheriae. Respiratory diphtheria can lead to severe complications, including airway obstruction and systemic toxin effects. Vaccination with diphtheria toxoid-containing vaccines has significantly reduced the incidence of this disease. The report emphasizes the importance of maintaining high vaccination coverage to prevent these diseases. It also highlights the need for ongoing surveillance and research to address challenges such as waning immunity and evolving epidemiology.
